utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you as well. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. Together with me is also Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, our case manager, and our consulting expert, Doctorandus Fagel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, good afternoon to you and your team, as well as to you, Mr. Fagel. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my learned friends from the Office of the Prosecutor and to all those present. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Geoff Roberts, and our expert, Mr. Esad Bilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good afternoon to you and your team, and to you, Mr. Bilic, as well. So, I take it that there are some preliminaries before we bring in the witness? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I request that Ms. Patricia Sellers to make a short submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The Prosecution would like to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention and also to our learned friends that there are several documents that we wanted to tender into evidence. One is the translation -- the new translation of P84, the corrected version. The others Prosecution Exhibit formerly numbered 598. What the Prosecution, with Your Honour's leave, would suggest is that we have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe it's 598, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: What we would suggest is if it is possible is hold a session in court, an administrative session, where these issues could be dealt with, and I understand there will be some corrections, for example, to transcripts and a couple of other documents we want to make sure are clearly placed on the record and any corrections that should be put there in are also noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your position on this, Ms. Vidovic? I would take it that in the case of the Defence, too, there are some clean-up measures that need to be undertaken still with regards to some documents? So if you both agree that there should be an ad hoc sitting or part of a sitting dedicated to this clean-up process. We are prepared for it and we will try to accommodate you, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honour. That would be helpful. However, as far as 558 [as interpreted] is concerned, I believe that this is the document that I objected to it being replaced by another. I, however, have to double-check this and I will do this in the meantime. If this is indeed 598, that is, then -- we still have to check of course. We'll see whether that's the document and it would be appropriate to do that at one such session. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Without pre-empting any issues of course, because these are pleasures still to come, we'll just agree here and now that as soon as we finish with this expert witness, we will then proceed with this cleaning process. I would suggest that in the meantime you have during breaks or whenever mutual consultations, at least to indicate the one to the other which documents you are meaning to refer to and - during this cleaning-up process. All right. And then we can proceed -- and also keep us informed. Thank you. Anything else? Yes, I recognise Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I just want to say that we will be in the touch with the Defence. There's also a 92 bis statement and we'll try to make the process not only as open as possibly but also that it runs smoothly in that we what to make sure that the documents are in their correct form. And just -- I see that Madam Vidovic on the record mentioned 558, and I just do want to confirm that it's 598 so that when she's looking at this document she'll know which one we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Any further matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's one arising in relation to this witness, which is that we've had disclosed to us two reports already prepared by this expert for the Office of the Prosecutor. We were informed, I think ti was today or yesterday that apparently there's another one, but in any event we were informed just before the hearing that that was placed in our locker at 1.45 p.m. I have to say, we're not delighted about it being placed in our locker at that stage because, in fact, first of all, we don't have it physically with us now. We were all up here in court at that point. And secondly, of course, we haven't had the opportunity to analyse it, to see it with our expert, and there might be matters arising from that report which, obviously, we want to put to the witness. So it's just to register that, and we will look at the report during the break, and if there's a great deal arising from that, then we may need to have a bit more time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. This is what you were talking about and you were even luckier than we were because we only received it on our way into the courtroom. So I don't know what is involved, but it seems to be something related to the French ministry of the interior and analysis -- but I don't know because, of course, we haven't had time to look at it, just as you haven't. But -- yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to support you on the information we disclosed earlier this month two reports, examination reports, established by Dr. Kerzan in the case of Brdjanin and Jevtic. Now, this information disclosed is an additional report and additional finding regarding this Jevtic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The additional report is by a French lab, they did a similar examination as Dr. Kerzan did, and also a witness had been heard and, of course, the sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That -- because I actually queried my mind: How does the ministry of the interior of the French Republic come into this matter? Although, of course, later on it shows that it is in relation to a request by an officer of the Prosecutor -- Office of the Prosecutor here. So let's bring -- any further matters, preliminary matters? No. Mr. Jones, Ms. Vidovic, are you happy with the seating arrangement?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We plan to consult, rather, during the break with our expert, rather than during the hearing, which might be a bit disruptive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. So let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon to you, Dr. Kerzan, and welcome once more to this Tribunal. We will soon with commencing with your expert testimony. In the meantime, I would kindly ask you to make the solemn - what's this? - make the solemn declaration pursuant to our Rules that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is, I see, in your hands already. Could you please read out that -- read it out loud and that you will be under -- your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Dr. Kerzan, there will be a few questions that we put to you already when you came here earlier on. We have to go through the same process again for the record. This is a proper sitting in which you are giving testimony, and therefore I will be proceeding with some questions which are a repetition of the ones that I put to you earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doctor, could you, for the record, kindly state your full name and your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: My name is Dorijan Kerzan. I was born on 16th of June, 1965, in Ljubljana, Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. And for the record, also, the way we are going to proceed is as follows. We will go -- first we will put all the questions that we have thought of to the expert witness, then Prosecution and the Defence will be given the opportunity to ask -- to put questions to the -- to Dr. Kerzan within the scope of his report and testimony, and that also means that it will be also within the scope of his testimony in response to the questions that we would have put to him in the meantime. There is something wrong? It's okay. I was -- I had -- yeah, it's not working properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's proceed not to waste time. Dr. Kerzan, I just want to confirm with you the following, namely, that you were, way back, appointed by this Tribunal as a signature expert in this case and that you have carried out this task and filed your report on the 20th of February of this year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could the usher kindly hand to the witness his report. And could you, Mr. Kerzan, confirm to us that this is indeed your report, after which we will introduce it in the records of this case.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, this is my report; it bears my signature or my stamp impression on every page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So that will become Court TC, Trial Chamber document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit C7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: C7. Okay. And the translation into English will become C7.E or E, C7E, and the -- into Serbo-Croat, if it goes into the record as well, as C7B? You have received the translation into Serbo-Croat in time to enable you to consult with your client, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Apparently there's been a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm working from the old one, since I marked that one-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've gone through the revised translation, and there are a few things but ...

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, about this translation, I would like to comment them because there are some slight misunderstandings. So I would like to comment on them later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay, we will please have the opportunity to do so as we go along. You have also brought back with you, I take it, the documents that we handed to you when you last came here?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And you have received -- taken re-possession of them, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kerzan, before we proceed any further, can you -- are you in a position to confirm to us that you carried out your assignment, your task, faithfully, honestly, and to the best of your ability?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is your present occupation, Dr. Kerzan?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I work as a forensic handwriting and document examiner, and I'm the head of the unit for forensic document and handwriting analysis at the forensic laboratory for -- of police of Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information. Now, you've reached a high position in your country in that laboratory?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: That would be the highest position in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you briefly describe to us the learning- and experience-gaining process that you had to go through in your field of expertise before you reached that position.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I was taken to the job in 1992, in 1st of July, 1992, as a beginner, of course. And right from the start, I started in-house training. In-house training is basically -- was basically at that time working cases under the -- under the supervision of -- of more experienced experts. In my case, that was Ms. Andrea Stegnar who actually taught me what I know now. I worked under supervision for four years. We do not have any -- at that time we did not have any exam at the end of it; it was just a mutual decision of head of handwriting and document unit, which was Ms. Stegnar, and the head of the lab that the expert is capable of doing expertise by himself. So we didn't have at that time any programme. We are currently working on a programme of training. That's how it started. In 1997, I became the head of department when Ms. Stegnar retired, and I'm the head of department since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. What does your role as head of department of director, as you put it before, imply by way of responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I'm not a director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: As head of department, I have to do all the paperwork, of course. I do the heaviest and most problematic cases, and of course I train people. I did train all of the -- all of the expert working in the -- in our lab currently. Currently I have two experts that work by themselves. One expert who is at the end of the training process, and one expert-to-be who started the training process approximately one year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Can you roughly but to the best of your knowledge, as accurately as possible, give us an indication as to how many signature examinations and analyses you have conducted in your career. Would we be talking of tens? Hundreds? Thousands?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, as an expert witness appointed by the court, which is the way I am appointed here, I did have the last five years around 70 expert theses; I wrote them and did the examination. As an employee of the police lab, I have -- now it's difficult to say, from 50 to 100 cases per year. So if we multiply that by 14, I would say, to be on the safe side, 700, and for which more than a half for signatures or probably even more so. It's rough to estimate. But together with handwritings it was far -- with handwriting, which does not really differ that much from the signature examination, it's well over 1.000 cases in 14 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. So do I take it therefore that you're not only or exclusively a signature examination or analysis expert but also a handwriting and document expert?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your training throughout the years included gaining expertise in examining handwriting, apart from signatures and also documents?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I got this training and I don't do cases in documents anymore because I don't have time. But I did a lot of it, and I'm also a currency expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A currency expert, yeah, you explained that. One related question just for our need to know this. Is it necessary for a signature expert to be also an expert in handwriting document examination?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Not in document examination, but certainly in handwriting examination. Handwriting examination and signature examination are two -- are actually one field, there's just small, small differences in the approach to the material. It is not necessary to be a document examination, but it can help sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you. Dr. Kerzan, are you familiar with the Serbo-Croat language and with the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To what extent, have you studied Serbo-Croat in --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I -- of course, basically, in former Yugoslavia all the non-Serbo-Croat citizens were basically bilingual. We had to learn Serbo-Croat in school, and my original university degree is in Slovene language, and within that we had also exams in Serbo-Croat or Serbian and Croat at that time already. So I can read and -- I can read. I wouldn't like to write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Dr. Kerzan, do you belong to any professional associations in your country or outside or abroad?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: In Slovenia we have no professional association of the kind, but I'm a member of European Network of Forensic Handwriting Examiners. And nothing else, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Have you published in the area of forensic sciences, in particular on signature examination?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote kind of a -- within a broad textbook of criminalistics and forensics, I wrote the introduction of handwriting and signature analysis, and I wrote some other, at least two I think, papers on signature and handwriting analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: -- among other things, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you ever given lectures on the subject?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your country or outside your country?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I give lectures each year for the new employees of criminal police. I did -- I did a lecture once in USA which was not very important, but not on a -- on the -- not always. I mean, I don't do that regularly, on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you participate in conferences in Slovenia or outside of Slovenia on --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Again -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: In Slovenia, there was no conferences yet about that, except probably in-house conferences. But I -- of course, I do. I go to the ENFHEX meetings, I was in the secret service meeting, and other meetings of handwriting. I can't attend all of them, I can't really attend all of them but I go to most of them, most of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And while we are on the same subject, have you ever been involved in examining or analysing signatures together with other experts from outside Slovenia, not from Slovenia in other words?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I think there were cases when in Slovenian -- Slovenian courts wanted outside experts, but to my knowledge I'm not really familiar with that. Because we don't follow the court procedure after we file --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean to say -- I don't think you got my question or my question was not clear enough. Did you ever carry out signature analysis or examination together with other -- other experts not from your country?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, okay. Now, have you personally, that is, as Dr. Kerzan, ever carried out forensic examination for any organ of this Tribunal until now or for any accused in front -- before this Tribunal or Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I have to clarify here. My lab was -- was called on twice to do examination of signatures and handwriting. I did that. I don't know in which -- for which part of this Tribunal, whether Prosecution, Defence, or anything. I -- once I did -- I did analysis with the help of my co-workers in the case when I had to exam the signatures of Dragan Jevtic. I have no idea who that is. I was told by the Tribunal representative it's -- has something to do with the case of General Krstic, I think, as far as I remember. It was quite some years ago. Then I was approached by another -- I mean, our lab was approached, to be precise, by Tribunal to -- just to clarify some documents in the case of Mr. Brdjanin, I believe. There are only three documents, and we were not able to produce any opinion at that time. And I was once called by phone from Den Haag to see a document to give some kind of linguistic opinion whether this is in Serbo-Croat or not, whether this resembles more like Albanian Serbo-Croat. I don't know what case that was. I just -- it was just a short talk with a person from this Tribunal when I clarify my -- I don't think that the text was written by -- I think it should be written by Serb, but there were so many funny words in between, that I assumed it is possible that it's an Albanian who wrote that. That was three cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in these three cases, you maintain that, in other words, you were not approached in your own personal capacity as an expert, but in your function as the head of the unit within the --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- forensic laboratory of the police.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Except for the last case, for all the others the lab was approached. I was just assigned by the head of the lab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's come to methodology. From a general approach, we'll come to more detailed matters later on, talking of methodology, could you briefly explain to us what is involved in the forensic examination and analysis of signatures.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, there are a couple of principles in signature and handwriting examination; they do not differ a lot. Excuse me. And basically that means -- it states that no two persons are writing completely alike, that nobody, when trying to imitate somebody else, is writing or -- a signature can do that as fluently as the person whose handwriting that actually is, and so on. All these are explained in my opinion. The methodology itself, the method we in our lab use is, I think, basically in - and I do use myself - is basically the same as everywhere in the world. What we do is in the first place -- in the first place I have to explain something. We try to find the traits of the handwriting or signature that differs from ideal -- ideal script. The ideal script we call which is the script which is taught in school so -- with the children. Children very early start to develop their own typical signature. I am currently working on a children's handwriting -- some kind of analysis. I hope to publish that later. And year -- at 10 years of age, the handwriting is very much already individual. So what we actually do is to see how in the way this handwriting, the handwriting of the person, changes from this ideal script. There are two types of -- at least two types of typical traits we are looking for. One are so-called general traits, which are the traits of -- the look of the handwriting or signature, the slant, the -- how big the -- how big the signature or handwriting is, the connections, is it connected or not, is it cursive or not. And the next step is to examine the detail -- the detail -- the detailed traits. For the first one, we usually do not use any particular equipment, except for magnifier, perhaps. For the later, for the detail, which means that -- details are usually the directions of strokes, the way the strokes are interconnected, there's many of that. There's the moment we need a microscope. I personally use a microscope with a magnification of 30 to 50 times, and here we can see how certain -- a certain sign was executed, because when you don't -- when you look at signs, at the signatures, at handwritings without a magnification, you can see the shape of it, while looking at it with a microscope, you see the way it is executed. It is very easy to explain that. You can have a loop written clockwise or counterclockwise, and you can -- very often you cannot see that with the naked eye, you have to -- you need the magnification, but you can see the slant of it, you can see whether it's open or not, whether it connects, whether it's -- there's many of those things that can be observed. You can also by -- what we also do is check any unusual traits in the handwriting or signature. Basically that means we are trying to find the -- any stops in the lines which are unusual, if there's stop -- stop of the writing line on the spot where it shouldn't really be. Of course, we also -- I mean, I also -- I also check the -- this -- you can also see the speed of writing by that, whether the lines are smooth, are -- whether the lines are dynamic, meaning that when person executes his handwriting or signature, the pressure of the writing utensil changes from stroke to stroke, and you can see that by microscope and sometimes by naked eye, but usually we have microscope and so on. So it's -- it's basically that these are the ways I do the -- the examination. Of course, within each -- within each examination you have to adapt to the material available, and then you -- I have to check what -- what can actually be examined in each particular case. Would that be in short?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you so much. Are there different methodologies in this area of expertise that you are aware of worldwide?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: For forensic handwriting and signature examination, I don't think so. There may be a difference in approach, but basic math that is, I believe, the same all over. There is not a big difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a difference in relation to the conclusions or scale of conclusions that one should aspire to arrive at or should strive to arrive at in analysing or in comparing signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, there are differences. There are differences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you explain these differences to us, please.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the different scales of conclusion here, but I remember that, for example, the United States secret service with whom I have -- who trained me a little bit years ago have nine -- nine points of a scale of conclusion, while FBI had, I think, seven. But basically that's only between certainty and probability to the inconclusive. So what they do is, at a certain point they are certain, then there's very probable, probable, inconclusive, and then the other way around for not -- for nonidentification of the handwriting or signature. What I use is the slightly modified scale of conclusion used by ENFHEX, this European Network and Forensic Handwriting examination -- Experts, are used in their collaborative exercises. I find it very good and I use then my personal, final opinion I put at the end of it. So the differences are, basically, that in some countries experts write their statement with full certainty, which means that they state: Somebody is the writer; while I believe -- I believe you can't say that. We can say that all the evidence within the handwriting or signature point to the fact that certain person is a writer. Therefore, I do -- in my opinion he is. But I try not to say there is something that is hundred per cent because there is nothing hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two short questions that arise out of the answer that you have just given. You mentioned in relation to the European Network collaborative exercises. Can you explain what these are and whether you have participated -- ever participated in any of them.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Those are -- the ENFHEX collaborative exercise, yearly collaborative exercise prepared by one of the European labs which is the member of the ENFHEX -- or, actually ENFSI, European Network of Forensic Science Institutes. The last one by Germans and before that by Swedes, and, yes, our lab participated in that and I do personally participate. I always did the collaborative exercise that arrived to our lab. It was six collaborative exercises, I think, up until now, five, six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you also stated in your previous answer that your methodology as regards scales is a slight modification of the European Network scale. Where does the slight modification --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will explain that to you. On page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dr. Kerzan, I see that you have a cold or you're not feeling a hundred per cent fit.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if at any time you need to have a short break or if you need any medication, aspirin, or anything, please do not hesitate to stop us.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, on the page 5 and 6 it says "analysis result scale," it's scales and conclusion. And I actually did use the -- everything from the ENFHEX scale until the last bolded sentence, which is in my opinion the question and so on. This is what -- this is the modification. The other parts are the same, except that the originals, it doesn't say assumption but it says proposition, and it doesn't say [indiscernible] but it is limitations and so on, but is it just a matter of words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So basically if we can conclude on this part, as your membership in the European -- of the European Network and participation in these collaborative exercises really impact on the methodology that you use in the signature examination and analysis?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Not the methodology itself I would say, but with a lot of participation in these meetings, with a lot of discussion with other experts, I think I became far more cautious than ten years ago, for example. So, yes, it did affect me a lot because these are very high-level meetings and with a very interesting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But is there such a thing as the "ENFHEX methodology"? Would you agree with me that there is such a thing or not?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I cannot answer really that. There are documents that help -- that help -- help expert, but, no, it's not a methodology. There are just papers of -- I don't know how they call it -- call them. It's -- actually out at this point say these are documents that Mr. Fagel there knows and he would say what kind of documents that are. These are documents that are published by the ENFHEX to help -- particularly in quality assurance and accreditation processes. It's not methodology, but it helps -- it helps a person to -- to be more precise and to give you some kind of guidance with the methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if I were to ask you then to briefly describe what is the contribution of ENFHEX to the science, to the forensic science of handwriting and signature examination and analysis, how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's -- well, ENFHEX organised, first of all, the conferences which are extremely important in our view. The last conference was in Budapest in November and it was extremely exciting. The other thing is ENFHEX in a certain way helps to unify approaches to handwriting and signature examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unify or standardise?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Standardise, yeah, standardise. That would be what ENFHEX actually does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So now we come to the task that you carried out for us. Before so doing, Madam Registrar, I think I need to have readily available to be shown to the witness all the documents that he made use of during his analysis and which he has now returned. And also we would need to have a look at them as we go along on the ELMO. All right. Okay. His report is in his possession or do you have it? I think they all need to be readily at hand, plus the English translation of the report.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I have my versions of report, which are on the same side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: So I don't really need that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you very soon, Dr. Kerzan, how you proceeded that to conduct the examination and analysis of the questioned signature, but before doing so I want to put my mind and that of my colleague and of everyone here at rest that in the course of your examination and analysis, you did -- you carried out same entirely by non-destructive and non-damaging means.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, I want your confirmation, a confirmation from you, that you have done nothing to the documents, both the questioned and the reference ones, which could affect their physical integrity.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, could you just explain to us exactly the procedure that you followed in carrying out and completing the exercise that we tasked you with.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, first at the beginning I, of course, see the -- I did -- I checked the reference material. I had eight referenced signatures at the top of the eight pages, which are described in the opinion and paper, and I assessed those signatures one by one. That means that I examined them and I took notes on every characteristics I notice on each particular, particular signature.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I did that for each particular reference signature separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Just by way of example, let's -- let's have reference signature with ERN 02066400 please put on the ELMO. No, no, it's the signature on the top left-hand corner. Yes -- yes, this is the signature from this document that you used as a reference signature?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, this was the first one I examined, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And would you like to see the other reference documents to confirm to us --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I have copies here for myself, so I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We could put on the ELMO the very first diagram, image 1, from his report. Page 18 in -- yeah, that's the one. And if it is in colour, it's much better. Okay. Now, could you explain to us -- for example, this is one -- this is the reference signature that I just referred to a minute ago. I see on this image here the signature with a number of arrows pointing at various parts of that signature. That is your work, I take it. Could you explain to us in -- briefly and in simple terms exactly what those arrows signify in relation to your analysis.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Well, arrows -- there are two arrows number 1. There's ones here and ones here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: You can see that yourself. Those are pointing to the two vertical lines which represent part of letter N in Cyrillic. Letter N in Cyrillic resembles or is similar to the letter H in Latin handwriting. The left one also shows the ending of the loop of sign O, which -- which penetrate -- the ending penetrates deeply into the loop and it actually goes over the line -- the left line of N. The number 2 arrows which are again two, are showing that the transcending line which connects the beginning and the end of the -- of the signature. Basically it's the vertical -- it's the horizontal line of N or H, N in Cyrillic, which connects also with the -- with the soft C as it is called, the C, at the end of the signature. Then number 3, arrow number 3, is showing the -- a little bit heart-like feature, feature at the beginning and ending as well of the O. We can see the beginning which is roughly over here exactly, and then it goes -- the loop is long -- it's quite big and long. Then number 4 is missing here, while number 4 later on is showing the -- the -- just a second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see an arrow with a number 4 here.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, it is. Sorry. I saw it. The number 4 shows the initial stroke of letter P, the beginning. It's not very well seen. It's far better seen with a microscope, but it -- actually P starts with an initial stroke and then it breaks down or it turns down sharply to the lowest point of P which is pointed by the arrow number 5. Line which has number 6 is showing, as it was in the translation, the wave-like parts of the signature which represents R. R in Cyrillic is the same as P in Latinic, and E -- no, Y, sorry. And Y, which is basically in Cyrillic the same as it is the turn-around N -- the turn-around N, but within the cursive writing it's just a wave. Then the 7 is actually showing the additional -- little additional feature which is before the -- actually C starts. I find this feature very interesting because sometimes it is within the -- the loop of C, sometimes before it. This is the actually additional -- additional trait. It does not correspond to any letter in this particular case, not in all case reference of material. Then that is number 7. Number 8 is showing the lower part of the first -- of the second stroke of H, and 9 is showing the finishing of the -- sorry, not H, C,. And the 9 is also showing the ending of the C. The same goes to -- applies to all of the -- of the signatures or images and annotations on the signature -- on the images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. And then after establishing these traits in the reference signatures you proceeded to --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: To the questioned signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to the questioned signatures. And what did the exercise that you carry out -- that you carried out actually consist? What did you do in trying to analysis?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I took exactly the same steps within the examination of the questioned signatures as within the examination of referenced signatures. Of course, I did not mention that before, I measured all those. I measured the length, the height, the axis -- let's see the English translation here. So I checked all those, and then -- for all of the signatures, questioned and reference. And then I approached the questioned signatures in the same way. First I checked the legibility, the appearance of it, and all the characteristics I could see without the microscope, and then I took the microscope and checked it with the microscope. Of course there were differences in approach for different questioned signatures, basically because the signature P3, questioned signature P3 is actually -- well, the document is a photocopy, including the signature, which can be easily proven. And I did not -- I did see only some similarities, but I could not establish all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: You'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. Before we proceed any further, did you obtain access or had access to either or both of the Prosecution and Defence expert reports at any time before or after your appointment by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I never saw those expert opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You refer in your report to a scale, which you also explain, analysis/results scale. We'll go through them one by one, and very shortly, for the record, could you explain to us what is meant by each of them. The first right up at the scale of these conclusions is conclusions strongly supporting the assumption that the questioned and reference signatures were written by the same individuals, which is followed then by your opinion that the questioned and reference signatures were written by the same person.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when would you reach such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: In what way "when"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When, under -- in which circumstances would you reach such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I would reach such a conclusion when there were no limitation to -- first of all, no limitation to the examination. It means that I have full visual access, if you want, to the handwriting or signature. I have to see all the features of the signature from the beginning to the end of the signature. There should be no -- when comparing the questioned -- questioned signatures to the -- to the reference signatures, there should be no similarity -- no differences which cannot be explained by the natural variation of the handwriting, which means certain differences in proportions, not a big differences. Those are depending also on the pre-printed symbols. There should be no different strokes, important strokes, and so on. And there has to be similarities, enough similarities to say that it is extremely unlikely that two -- that another person would write exactly in the same way. In the -- well, that would be about that, if that's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And the second conclusion in this scale would be conclusions support the assumption that the questioned and reference signatures were written by the same individual. And your opinion would be then that the questioned and referenced signatures were probably written by the same person. How would this -- explain this, please, but explain in particular how would this differ scale-wise from the previous conclusion.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, previous is basically a conclusive opinion, while the second is qualified opinion, I would say. I believe that within the second point on a scale of conclusions, I can say that there are similarities, but due to different factors I cannot be certain that the person -- that this is the person. That can be either because of simplification, it can be either because of the signature's implication of the signature. It can be either because of the limit -- certain limitations, if the part of the signature is not very well visible. And there can be, of course, that some trait on the signature does not really correspond fully to the reference signatures. That would be the moment when I would decide for this -- for this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I will ask you the question now; I meant to ask it later on, but since you've mentioned the term. I will put it now. You referred to simplification of the signature. What do you exactly mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, the signature -- particularly the signature which is highly symbolised, meaning that it's not legible, it's just a way of symbols you cannot really read what it is. In this case is this signature's -- even when person is signing document after document, the signature is losing the characteristics. The certain -- for example, when you have wavy lines in the signature, then they can become straight and so on. That would be simplification, if that answers you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next down the scale is inconclusive. What -- when would you come to had that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: That conclusion -- inconclusive, not really a conclusion anyway, it's when there are some similarities and there are also differences, and I can -- and due to the different factors, I cannot assess whether they -- whether they point to one or the other proposition, either the person wrote or did not wrote the signature or handwriting. That would mean that there's not enough evidence to any of the proposition or it could mean that the signature -- the actual examination was not possible due to severe limitations. That part is not written into the report, I have to admit. When the examination is -- has limitations like bad photocopies, faxes, or that there is very -- some strong stain over the handwriting or the signature, then you cannot see enough of the signature or you can't see enough traits detailed. In this case, you -- the expert should decide the result of the examination as inconclusive. It cannot -- that does not of course mean that the person did not or did write, we just cannot find evidence to support any of those propositions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Dr. Kerzan. And next down the scale is -- there are two more. The first one is conclusions support the assumption that the questioned and reference signatures were not written by the same individuals. And the opinion would be that the questioned and referenced signatures were probably not written by the same person. When would you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, it would be similar as the point 2 on the scale of conclusions. When the -- in the case when I do not find enough differences to be -- to be, to a certain extent, certain about that, then I would say probably the person did not write that. I -- in this case, I just leave the floor to the possibility that something happened while writing or signing certain documents, and that's why I couldn't prove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I come to the last part of the scale, and I draw your attention that at least our attention has been drawn to some fault in the translation into English in this paragraph. Basically I'm told, before I proceed with the question, that the second sentence which presently reads: "The questioned and reference samples contain many major differences," should read: "Between the questioned and reference samples, there are" --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: If I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: "Many significant differences."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no major similarities between them, and then after that that there are many significant differences, and then it follows after that, there are no major similarities between them. All right. So my question to you in regard to this scale: Conclusions strongly support the assumption that the questioned and reference signatures were not written by the same individual, and I notice the extra words "strongly support" now. And your opinion would be now at this point that the questioned and referenced signatures were not written by the same person. When would you come to that conclusion therefore?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I would come to the conclusion if I did not find any real similarities between the -- between the questioned and reference material. Basically within the scope of the signature examination, it usually means that a person -- that somebody is trying to -- not to imitate somebody else's signature, but he just wrote the signature with -- in handwriting. So that would be a -- just to explain how that -- how this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Dr. Kerzan. I will now lead you through various parts of your report, and specifically refer to the various documents that you have examined. I will start first with the so-called reference documents which I made reference earlier on. And for the record, I'm referring to documents from ERN 02066400 to 407, that is eight documents in all. Dr. Kerzan, you have examined these documents and you give your opinion in regard to them in pages 7 and 8 in the English text of your report and come to certain conclusions, particularly that all the individual features that you identified and which you explained or indicated to us earlier on are sufficiently distinct to make analysis and comparison possible. Can you kindly, briefly explain to us your findings in regard and what you mean by this. Particularly my first question would be the following: When you analysed all these eight reference signatures, do you come to the conclusion that they are signed by the same person, to start with.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes. To answer this question, yes, I come to the conclusion that the same person wrote them. At this point I would just like to correct a couple of things in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: So the examination -- this is the -- when it starts: All the reference signatures are written in the upper portion of the documents. The next sentence is, this being the case the top edge of the sheet of a paper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hold it, you need to tell us the page, please.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Page 7, line 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 -- line 10 and 11. It says: "This being the case, the top edge of the sheet of the paper and the straight pre-printed lines in the document had to be taken into account." It misses here, taken into account as what? As a base line. The same goes to the B/C/S translation, the B/C/S translation. May I say what should state here in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I will read the sentence as it should be written. [Interpretation] "one should look at the top page of the paper. There are lines on the paper which serve as the base line of the signature." This part was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that. Any further comment in relation to the text?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. Later on when I describe ratio. It's eight lines further down. The sentence says: "The ratio show between the length of the signature and the transverse line is approximately 1 to 2, nearly 1 to 1." "It ranges from 1 to 2 to 1 to 1," it should be said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ranges.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: While interestingly enough in B/C/S translation it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Any further comment you would like to make in regard to this part of the report?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Should I go to the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because the next page deals with the --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: -- with the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- with the reference documents.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: First of all, the translator used work "breaking." The word "breaking the line" could mean that the line completely stopped and then there is another line. It should probably say the change of direction of the stroke in this particular cases, not break the stroke. If you say "break the stroke," it would be cut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Broke --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: In eighth -- in eighth line it -- it is the sentence "descending is relatively deep," and then something, "and can intersect the left -- from the left with the two vertical lines." I would say it's -- it intersects the vertical -- it covers the vertical line, it can cover the vertical line of N, that's on figures 1, 2, and 4, when that's -- actually covers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: And even more important is three lines below it says "it starts at the top with two initial strokes." That's not so. That's completely wrong. The Cyrillic symbol for -- for R or P, as it looks like, it starts at the top twice with initial strokes, twice on this reference material there are initial strokes. On the -- you can see them on figure 1, as it says here, if you check that. It is seen -- this is not very well seen, it's arrow 4 on figure 1, and it is barely seen on figure 5. I did not put an arrow because it's in -- only with the microscope. The initial stroke traces -- the next stroke, it traces the initial stroke. That's quite a big difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: And then a couple of lines later on it says: "The vertical is relatively deep and low. Sharp, but rounded." It's not sharp but rounded. It's sharp or rounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, it's not sharp --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's one or the other. It can can't [Realtime transcript read in error "can"] be sharp and rounded at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How should it read? The vertical is relatively deep and low?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Sharp or rounded and open then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And breaking, you said --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Turning down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Turning --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: -- it's changing direction. Can I do the same for the Bosnian/Serbian/Croat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, go ahead. I don't understand the Serbo-Croat --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it would be proper to do that. It's -- I will say -- only one of those mistakes happens in B/C/S. Approximately in the middle of the page the sentence in B/C/S reads: [Interpretation] "This ending is relatively deep and can interact with two verticals to the left," whereas actually it should read: "This ending is relatively deep and should intersect or interact with the left vertical." [In English] -- find all the things that I don't agree with in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio MR. DI FAZIO: I think there's just a typo, at page -- previous page, 32, line 20, 22 it appears the witness said "it can be sharp and rounded at the same time." I think he meant the opposite, it can't be sharp and rounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it anyway. I mean, I wasn't following the -- the transcript but that's how -- it's either one or the other.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So going back to my question I asked you a few minutes ago -- let me -- so my question to you, to bring everyone back to -- in line is the following. I said: "Dr. Kerzan, you have examined these documents and you have given your opinion in regard to them on pages 7 and 8 in the English text of your report, and come to certain conclusions, particularly that all the individual features that you identified and which you explained to us earlier on when I was referring to image 1 in your report, you explained or indicated to us, are sufficiently distinct to make analyse and comparison possible." This is your conclusion. And then I said: "Can you briefly explain to us your findings in regard, and what you mean in this. Particularly, my first question to you was the following," to which you answered yes. "When you analysed all eight reference signatures, do you come to the conclusion that they are signed by the same person to start with?" And your answer was: "Yes." So having come to that conclusion, can you explain to us what message you mean to convey to us when you say that they had individual features which are sufficiently distinct to make analysis and comparison possible. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, as you have read in my opinion, I -- basically I describe the features from one letter to another, from one sign to another, within -- also bearing in mind that these signs or letters are all in Cyrillic script. I don't know if it's necessary, but, for example, for the letter on N which is within the loop of O is basically composed of three writing strokes, one is very long, and so on. For each feature I did -- for each part of the signature, I did the same, I described it. And all these features together present a distinctive signature identity. So all of those together are enough for expert to -- to -- to be able to present certain conclusions when comparing to the other signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please bear with us when I ask you these questions. I mean, we have, of course, read your report thoroughly and we know that this is explained in some detail in the report, but these are also public hearings, public sessions, and we need to ensure that whoever is following the proceedings from outside these four walls will be able to do so and understand exactly why you come to certain conclusions and not others.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Would that be then necessary to describe every --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that, again, if we show you, say, image 1 or you choose any of the eight reference signatures, you point to us what these distinctive features that enable a comparison are. I mean, that's -- would help the public understand better. Usher, if you can help --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I can use my copy, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we need to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's very randomly I took that one out. It's ERN --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Image 7.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Image 7, 02066406, for example. In this particular reference one of the features is missing, so I'll present it later on. You can see, as I showed on the letter, letter O, which is rounded, is -- it has a heart-like shape, it has a relatively -- not that deep penetration into the loop. If I may show the other one which is below image 8, it shows extremely long penetration into it, and this is the line which very often intersects with the left vertical of N. Now, to go back on image 7. Then this is the long line on N, which is intersecting the complete signature and finishing far away. Then you have P, the waves over here. The interesting inside -- inside feature within the loop of C, this one is very interesting, the same -- this is very -- there is more of this in the reference material. And then the other features, the downward stroke of the H and then the -- turning up and then again down. You can see basically also the slant which can be shown by that. I don't have the utensil to measure it here, but it's -- you can be sure that it was measured okay. So I don't know what to point to more -- of course, I can also show another page. Again, the one that we saw before, to show you it's arrow number 4, to show you, hardly visible initial stroke. Just a second, if I have a better image here. I apologise to be slow. Yes, I have a better image here, actually. These are the working images I used to -- you can see over here there is an initial stroke. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one is this image number?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: This is the first one, it's image 1. Image 1. It's this arrow 4 which presents the initial stroke of P, and it's -- it is seen -- it is not seen as good as when you use a microscope, but it is here and on this image it can be seen a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: You can also see that it's a light -- relatively light stroke so the parts of O which it covers is lighter in comparison to the other parts of O, if you want to do -- to see here when it goes on. I hope I explained that clearly enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Did you also compare the size of each of these reference signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did compare them. Yes, of course. I measured them, and they -- they are different, of course, but they are within the -- within the limitations of actual space they have. For example, image 2 you can see there's a lot of thods [phoen] because of the photocopy and the person signing that had far less place so he -- so this one is shorter, that's the reason why it's shorter and a little bit more simplified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then, Dr. Kerzan, you then proceeded, I take it, to examine the so-called questioned signatures, and my first questions -- question to you is the following. I take it that you did so separately, one by one?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you also in this process try to compare the various questioned signatures together?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: You mean questioned signature to questioned signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, not deliberately, but I did, actually, yes. I did not take one and the other and compare them to the others. But, of course, during the actual examination, of course one comparison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I must -- I've asked you this question because I do have a pertinent question later on in relation to one of the documents or one of the signatures. Could the usher please make available to the witness P3, the first of the questioned signatures. And could we put it on the ELMO, focussing and zooming in the signature part. Yes. Perfect. Now, Dr. Kerzan, this is the first of the 11 questioned signatures that you examined. I'm not saying that -- first for the purpose of this exercise, let's put it like this. And according to your report, after carrying out the comparative analysis or examination, you came to the conclusion that the examination of this signature is inconclusive. Can you briefly explain to us why you came to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, it is quite obvious that this document in its entirety is a photocopy. You can see that on the image I pointed to the certain deposits of dry toner, which I have to say there is a mistake in B/C/S translation. It says here, I do apologise, but I have to do that. It says [Interpretation] "Dried-up toner" it says, whereas it should say "dry toner." Therefore, the term "dried-up" in my opinion would mean it became dry, whereas it was dry in the first place, to begin with. [In English] And to go further with the signature itself, half of the signature is covered with what it seems like to be a stamp impression. So what one can see are only hints of a first part of signature. You can't see the R, at least I don't see it. I can see the lines that could relate to R, but I'm not sure that they are. There are some similarities in the ending of the signature, but it is far from enough to say that this is possible to do the examination. This -- in my opinion, this document is not -- is not good enough to make an examination. So the findings were inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. We come now to the next document, P4.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: If I just can make some order here in my documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I have three lines of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Wubben, Madam Vidovic, we will have a break in seven minutes' time, or something like that, eight minutes' time, after which I don't think that our questions will last too long. I reckon then within three-fourths of an hour after we recommence, we reconvene, we will be ready. So Prosecution is going first.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. P4.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, P4 is -- okay, the document was typed with a type-writer. It's what we call an original document not in any kind of a copy. You can see the signature is very nicely visible, despite the fact that a small part of the -- of the signature is covered by the stamp, but because of the different material it is nicely seen. It is written with -- by the fountain-pen, I reckon. And I see, and I have shown, the different -- the similarities to the reference material. It goes the same as the reference material with inside of N and long transpence [sic] line, the R, the waves, and so on. The difference which is interesting is the dot at the end of it, at the end of the signature, but I attributed this difference to the time, quite a lot of time, quite a lot of time elapsed between the questioned and the reference material. So I don't think it's that significant that I could not make my decision that findings strongly supported a proposition that -- to find that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just to clear this up straight away, at this point we come to this dot, another questioned document, to which reference is made later on, and in each case you come to the same conclusion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, that you attribute this dot to -- or this variance, in other words, to the lapse of time.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is also interesting that this dot only on -- only is seen on the dot -- on the signatures which are written by a fountain-pen. It's also interesting observation, I would say. And one of those does not -- does not have this document, it's P158. So I -- I didn't [Realtime transcript read in error "did"] find that very significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your experience is there a reason why there should be a dot behind a signature and why sometimes there should be one and sometimes not?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I don't have an idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your conclusion in regard to P4, you have explained basically the fact that there is a dot does not change the conclusion that the questioned signature was written by the same person as the reference signature. MR. DI FAZIO: Another one of those typos, if Your Honours please, I don't know if it's significant. Page 40, line 12, "I did find that very significant."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I did not find. MR. DI FAZIO: I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there is that arrow there. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I didn't realise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So my question to you is the following, that notwithstanding the fact that there is this dot behind the signature in this document, and I'm referring to this document only for the time being now, you did not come to the conclusion -- you did not arrive at the second part of the scale, you went right up to the highest. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And why would that be so?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Because this dot, it is -- it is, in my opinion, not significant. It is the dot that appears. This dot is possibly part of the signature, but it's not necessarily. It can also be a dot to show somebody where to sign, but in this case I don't think so, that it is. I think it's a variant of the signature of the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We come to P13, usher, please. Now, we, in relation to this document, you come to the conclusion of the second step in scale, namely that the questioned signature on this document was probably written by the same signatory as on the reference signatures. I -- you use in your report in relation to this document the simplification of signature, which you explained earlier on. Now, could you give us an illustration of the simplification of this signature that you see on the monitor now.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The simplification goes -- is within the letter Y -- E, sorry, excuse me. Letter E. It is not executed completely as you see. It is just one wave in the place where there should be two for -- to have a complete letter E. There are also two things -- another thing that I notice on this particular signature. There are some dots of -- some larger dots of the ink on it, which is probably due to bad ball-point, but also this shows -- it tells me that I cannot be as certain as the previous to the proposition that the same person wrote that. So I went one step below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And you also referred to your -- in this part of your report in relation to this document to a presence of ink spots.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you meant --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- by ink spots?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And looking at the stamp.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Stamp is so barely visible, so it does not limit the possibility of examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the fact that the stamp seems to be in purple or more or less similar to the ink used for the signature, does that interfere in any way?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't because it is different. I can clearly see the difference in colour, so it's -- and I also could have -- I did also use the police lab machine for that just to be sure. I did not mention in my report. I checked the line also on the VSC-2.000 in my lab. I did that with the permission of my head -- head of department, to check it out just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you explain precisely what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: With the ER elimination, you can divide the different colours of the ink so it's clearly dividable. I did not -- because it is the machine of the police, I did not present it here inside, but it's clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And with that we stop here for half an hour, 30 minutes. Yes, Mr. Wubben?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to make a short submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime I think the witness can be escorted and make sure that he has an ample supply of coffee.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I leave this stuff here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest you take it with you, Dr. Kerzan. I mean, I would rather not take responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For just so many papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I want to convey that I just signed a letter with a few pages, also to disclose -- in addition to the disclosure of this morning. It is related to the handwriting samples of that same examination, and I want to further clarify because that will also support the quick reading by the Defence, expeditious reading by the Defence of the material. The material that we disclosed the French report is this: The Kerzan report, the Kerzan report in the Jevtic case we disclosed earlier this month, and the French report analysed the handwriting and signatures of a document and reached the same conclusion, so both reached the same conclusion, namely that the handwriting and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. I mean, you don't have to tell us. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, I would like to confirm that for the record, Your Honour, namely that the handwriting and signature came from a man called Jevtic. Now, a Prosecution witness later claimed that he had authored the text, whereas Jevtic only signed the material. And I would like to refer, for a quick reader, to the transcript in English page 10 up to 15, and that's the reason why we disclosed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just to support Your Honours and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much. We will have a full 30, 30 to 35 minutes' break. And then the idea is to try and finish around about 5, 5-ish, 5.00 to 5.15 today. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next in line is P14. Now, there are a few things that I would like to explain. Basically, just for the record, your conclusion is more or less - I'm using my own language rather than yours - but some features are pointing to the possibility that the signature was copied or may have been copied, but -- although this cannot be conclusively stated. As a result of that, you come to the conclusion that the examination is inconclusive. Is that correct? Do I read you well or not?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Let me just read that. Yes. That would be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You referred to two unusual pen lifts --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in -- and there are seven strokes in this signature, whereas in the reference signatures you usually find five rather than seven. Although on a general basis, the features of the questioned signature do resemble those of the reference signature, you still come to the conclusion that you cannot come to a conclusion or that it is inconclusive. I think this is one of the documents that needs somewhat deeper explanation on your part.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I very much agree with you, Your Honour. So, as you might have seen on -- can I give the image -- my images on ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It would be better. It's easier to show an image than -- that's P14 here. Now, this image, this first image, image number -- on this one I don't have numbers. Image number 12, it is image number 12, yes. On image number 12 I've shown the features on this signature that correspond to the -- to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reference --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: -- reference material, although it has to be stated right away that this is extremely simplified version of the -- this kind of a -- of a signature because you can see that E is not visible at all, except for this little dot, tiny dot, tiny part here. Now, if I go further on, it's -- I won't go into details about these features we discussed on other.
