But then I took the microscope, and what came up is this very odd, odd stop of the line over here and beginning here. There are some hints of something else down there. There's some blue-ish colour over here. I don't know what it is. I was thinking of possibility that this is a striation mark. Striation mark is the mark of the ball -- the little ball on the ball-point. But this cannot be a striation mark, as you can see how the striation mark actually looks like. It's here. This is a striation mark. So there is an abrupt stop in the new beginning of the line. This is not something I would say usual for any -- any signature. Of course, there might be explanation for that. There might be a surface that stop the -- the pen, the writing utensil. There might be a hole in the surface, whatever. There are some possibilities, although with this very smooth lines here, I'm kind of worried that there's no such explanation. I believe this is a deliberate stop here; I don't know why. I can't explain it why. And again on the other -- on the next image I'm showing, it's not that well-seen on the image. That's the course of a digital photography. It probably would be better if I use a film. You can see there's one line and there's another line to the opposite direction. There are no such lines at -- at the reference material and, for that fact, any of the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Questioned --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: -- questioned documents. Those two features, one shown on an image 12B and 12A, are so strange that I went to the inconclusive. The fact that I didn't say it is a falsified -- falsified signature, that it is a forged signature is -- comes to the fact that there -- it's just too easy to be a forgery, I think. It's -- and it's only here. For a forgery, I believe there should be more so I couldn't really decide whether this is a forgery or not. That is the reason why I wanted -- I decide for inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: But it was very, very -- it gave me a lot of thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay. And when you said the seven strokes instead of five, going back to 12, if you could explain which are the seven strokes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Can I show you the first strokes on one of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: This is the first of those. You have one stroke. One is the loop, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Then there's two and three. Then four, it goes all the way here. This is four and this is five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Strokes in this meaning is the uninterrupted line of -- of the signature. And now here we have one is the loop and probably one even more here -- but I think that could be a problem of the ball-point. Because one is the loop. There are two inside the loop. Then there is four, the horizontal line. Five is this one here. Then you have six going up to the stop, and seven is -- is that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: These are seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me see if I had the questions to -- are there otherwise -- when you look at the stamp covering part of this signature, looking at that stamp, did it constitute any obstacle to you in trying to come to your conclusions or not?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Not to my conclusions. It was more difficult to show you this feature here, this double line in P -- in R, sorry. But otherwise, no. No, it's very -- it's hardly visible, this type of impression is not a very strong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next -- I lost my pen. I have another one here. Let's go to P37, please.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes, can I go just a little bit back. I had to comment on here. P14 down, on the fourth line from the down it says: "The next stroke flows downwards before it breaks downwards." It was my mistake. I omitted this. It was -- if it goes downwards, it then does not break downwards, it then opens again upwards. I just wanted to make that clear. It's also in the original, so it's something I missed when I was reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. P37. In here you come to the conclusion that the features of the questioned signature do resemble reference signatures. Some features are such that the result of the exam and your opinion is inconclusive. And that's the -- that is the conclusion that you reach.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your considerations, you also make reference to one -- at least one unusual pen lift at the I, where the I of Oric is, and that you also comment that the signature is larger than the reference ones and deviates significantly in the proportion from the reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: This you have non-amended version. This is the biggest mistake in the translation. It does not say that way. It does not deviate significantly. It says the -- in proportion. This is the mistake that was the most severe. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact now I refer to the -- parties to page 12 of the report, 11 lines into paragraph five where it says: "The signature is larger than the reference one, it also deviates significantly in proportion." I am told that the part reading "it also deviates significantly in proportion," should read: "Although the proportions do not differ essentially from the reference signature." Mr. Wubben, Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic, all right? Yes, so, of course -- I mean, taking this into consideration, we still remain with the fact that the signature is larger than the reference one. Does this really mean anything or does it carry any significant weight --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in trying to analyse the two?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think it's very significant. It's just my observation. It is larger, but the proportions are basically within the limitation of the -- of the -- of the reference signatures. The point that is larger is probably -- can come from the fact that the signer had more space to do anything or he signed in a different position. It's not very significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Sorry. And this pen lift at the I, where the I is, could you perhaps show it to us using your own image.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I will show it to you, I will try to explain it also. Well, you can see that the point -- I will tell you exactly what it is. You said 37. It is between the -- the N and A in the -- when you have down there written Naser, between A and N. N is here and A is here. This part is -- this is clearly a pen lift -- actually, the new beginning of the line. It's not probably a pen lift, but it's -- the line stopped, the pen was lifted -- you don't see the pen lift, you see the -- actually, the pressure down again. This is where it is. It goes down and I don't really know -- it could be here, too, because there is no -- there is no connection. That can be attributed to different factors. It can be, of course, that in this part somebody was trying to draw a signature. It also can be that the ball-point didn't work and that the person just -- just tried to make this trait visible, this line. There's two possibilities, I believe, at least. So -- but it does mean that something is not clear with this signature, in my opinion. And if -- if it's not clear, I can -- I cannot say it is a -- I cannot make an actual opinion. I think it's inconclusive because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I thank you. And again in this regard -- in regard to this document, again I would like to ask you about the -- how much of -- of a -- a problem was or wasn't, the purple stamp ink.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case a purple stamp ink was a bit stronger, but still the lines are visible anyway, not as clear on some others but are clear enough to see where the line stops, where the line begins, the stroke begins, the -- so on. It's mostly visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And compared with the stamp in the previous document, P14.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, the -- on P14 the stamp is not as strong. It does not cover so much of the signature where it's -- where it is in ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now we come to P73, and this is a signature which you state in your report is made with a fountain-pen, using a fountain-pen. You come to the conclusion that "findings strongly support the proposition that the same person wrote the questioned and the referenced signatures, therefore the questioned and reference signatures have been written by the same person." So you are back to the top of the scale when it comes to this signature.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, let's start with -- you have got nothing to add with regard to the point that appears or the dot that appears --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- after the -- no, you don't. So you stand by your statement -- your previous statement?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is in that particular document, if we can zoom out on this document, please. Zoom out completely.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: This is the most I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I have the document here, please? I think it's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can hand the document back to the witness. I refer you specifically to the stamp, which to me appears to be somewhat bolder, stronger, when it comes to ink content.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it does cover the initial part of the signature covering the O, the N, the Cyrillic N, and also part of the R.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The ascending part or descending part of the R.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You come to the conclusion that you are -- that the covered part is clearly visible and the stamp does not obstruct the examination. Do you stand by that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, using the magnifier, you can see clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can see --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's very, very clear by using a magnifier to see the difference between one and the other ink. It is seen clearer. It is also far better seen on my image than on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, can we see your image, please?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You can see -- does it do that automatically? I'll try to zoom it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Zoom it in, exactly.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: You can see here the particular lines -- you see the -- this line where here -- here you can see at the beginning of the -- of the R, it goes down here, not up here, and then further on. It is visible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, for example, if you were to assess or -- the speed of that particular part, would you be able to do that or not?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would be because you can see it, that the R line down is getting lighter here. It's not because of the stamp impression. It is actually getting lighter, so the pressure is not as strong as it is. But of course with a fountain-pen it is more difficult to see the -- the pressure as with a ball-point pen because the fountain-pen has liquid ink which is just pouring out of the pen, while here you have to move the ball of the ball-point to get ink on the paper. It has to -- the striation marks from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can the witness be shown the next document which is P74, please. Again, you come to the conclusion here, sir, that the findings strongly support the proposition that the same person wrote the questioned and referenced signatures, and therefore you come to the conclusion that the questioned and referenced signatures were written by the same person. In this case I will start with the stamp again. The stamp covers half of the signature, almost entirely the R, the Cyrillic R.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It covers three of the letters, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So you still maintain that that was not an obstacle for the -- to you for the examination?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, because with the magnifier -- while magnifying you can see this, and again I can show you on the image. I will also show you my image, and just do not change it. You can see all the -- all the strokes. All the strokes are visible here, the beginning of the stroke, and then you can see also the lighter stroke over here up -- so you can see what was supposed to be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything in this signature that relates to speed that you did not find in other signatures? Does it -- what are the indications as regards speed in this signature?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Again, it is fountain-pen. It is more difficult to assess the speed of the writing, but again you can see -- now I have those lines here. You can see that -- the thinner line here, which means that the pen was a little bit easier on that -- so it means it went faster, which is typical of the -- of the -- of those straight lines. And again the same goes up here. The others, the wavy lines, are more like -- are more like -- they are in the same speed. There's no speed -- there's no acceleration of speed as here, I think it is. And you have also here a little bit of -- it goes up -- it's -- it slows down and indeed increases speed again and so on. And you can see exactly here how pen was slightly lifting from the beginning -- from here to the other way. I think it's -- dynamics is seen enough, good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anything in this -- or any indication in this signature in relation to speed that singles it out when compared with the other questioned signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I don't find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially the ones with -- with -- written with a fountain-pen?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I don't find anything significant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: -- in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to P75, please.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: This is P75, I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, the next one we are going to see is P75.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again your conclusion here is that the findings strongly support the proposition that the same person wrote the questioned and reference signatures, and therefore the referenced and questioned signatures have been written by the same person, in other words, the highest grade in the scale that you mentioned. Can I have the document brought to us for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to give you back this document, and I need you to explain two things. There is some -- what appears to be some handwriting in the second line from the bottom of the written text above the signatures. And there is also what appears to be a typewriter correction in item number 1 of this document. Have a look at both first, and then I will ask you my questions. You say -- it's obvious that with regard to that typewriter correction, even to the naked eye, that seems to be correcting fluid --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and new words typed over the correcting fluid. When you say in your report here and in other places "there's no trace of manipulation or tampering with this document," what do you actually mean?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I mean that I don't feel somebody would deliberately change the document. This is, in my opinion, just typewriting error which was corrected. I did not find it that important to notice that, to be honest. And, of course, you have to realise that it's during the whole word that's written again, it's just the middle portion of the word. This was written over, I believe, before that, in that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And let's -- usher, please, could you show the witness P73.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, even that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, as you see that there is "Skelani" or "Skelana" in P73. We need -- it's another document. Do you find it?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I would say you would want -- you are talking about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, and there's something underneath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Again, when you say there is no trace of manipulation or tampering, did you take that into consideration or did you ignore it?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I did not take that into consideration; I ignored that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: This one I did not notice, to be honest. I was preoccupied with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I just want you to testify the truth; that's all. All right. So we come back to P75, please. You can remove P73. Your findings are based on the fact that the features of the questioned signature are very similar to the referenced signatures and that the presence of a point at the end of the signature does not change your evaluation or your assessment. Neither, I take it, does the fact that, although to a minor extent, the stamp covers part of the signature, do you -- does it?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to page 158.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Can I just have a comment on P75?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: The only of these signatures that does not have the initial stroke in the R, which is consistent with the -- with most of the reference material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, it doesn't change your --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P158, and your conclusion is, again, the highest level in the scale, highest grade, findings strongly support the proposition that the same person wrote the questioned and referenced signatures, therefore the questioned and referenced signatures have been written by the same person. My question rather relates now to a comparison between this signature in P158 and the other questioned signatures. Do you see or detect any particular variations or difference between this one and the other questioned signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: There is a slightly harder pressure on the two vertical -- verticals in P, but not a big one. There is no dot at the end of it, nothing which could not be explained by the natural variability [Realtime transcript read in error "ability"] of the handwriting or the signature. Natural variability, not ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we come to P210. Your conclusion -- this is -- let's say it straight away. This is a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not an original. And your conclusion here is that the findings are inconclusive. I would like you to explain why, and in particular how you come to this conclusion even when, according to you, the photocopy is of a relatively good quality.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, the fact that the photocopies is of good quality means that there's no extra dry toner deposits, comparing to P3, I think it was, also for the copy. For the copy P3 was a very -- relatively bad, bad quality in this case. But still, in this particular signature you have covered virtually the first two letters, the O and the N with the stamp impression and you can hardly see the beginning of R and the ending of R -- the lower portion of R. So I personally believe that that limits the possibility for examination so far that I cannot put it. Or to put it in the other words, sometimes, but very rarely, you can do a report on the photocopy. In my personal opinion, photocopies are not to be used in -- for expert's opinion. I usually decline that but -- I mean, I usually don't come to the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And the last document. This, as you rightly indicated in your report, is the only document which purports to have both the first name and the surname and the signature -- forming the signature. Your conclusion is that it is not possible to perform examination according to the standards that you adopt and that your findings are, therefore, inconclusive. I would like you or I invite you now to tell us all you can in relation to this document, which is even to the naked eye different from all the others.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, this document is a faxed document, which I think that is quite clear. You can see that by, as it says on the English translation "dashy edges," actually on the B/C/S translation the word is, I think, far better, but I don't find another one. It's a faxed message. It's an old-type fax, so it's analog fax, which I don't really know how it works, but new faxes work as a -- as a printers. They scan the document and put it into a digital message and send it through. This one is analog one, the old one with a thermal -- some kind of thermal -- thermal printing. This is the first observation. The second observation, as you've already noted it, it is the only signature which comprises of surname and given name. So I cannot compare this kind of signature to the signatures which do not contain the given name; it is impossible because it's a different. I've seen -- I've checked the document. It is possible that this document was sent to some headquarters in Sarajevo, I think. I've seen that on the document, I believe, so perhaps somebody who wouldn't usually sign with the name, given name and surname, would for the importance of the document or whatever write it that way. There are some differences in a situation when one does sign a document. So -- but nevertheless, most of the -- at least 50 per cent of -- all of the appearance of the signature is covered by the stamp impression. The fax is even of a poorer quality than the -- than the photocopy. It is -- it is a matter of doctrine, to put it that way, not to identify anything on the fax machine. Fax -- faxes are -- particularly those kind of faxes, this thermal faxes, are completely insuitable for handwriting or signature examination. That's why I went into the inconclusive conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You also mention in your report that there is no N, Cyrillic N, inside the O, as in the reference signatures. But is this of any relevance since the name and surname are signed separately or not one superimposed, not one inclusive of the other? You wouldn't expect it?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, actually I don't know. You wouldn't expect it because the actual signature, if we go to the reference signatures, these are nicely balanced, very nicely executed signatures. And the fact that the signature is executed with a N -- with the two strokes of N within the loop of O and then a long vertical. This is a very distinctive feature, so -- but I have no idea whether there are some possible reference materials that are written in this way so -- with a surname and given name. So it's hard to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much, Dr. Kerzan. I -- we don't have any further questions for you. Now, what's going to follow is a series of questions from Mr. Wubben, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- who is going to put the questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't stated anything in confirmation in that respect, but I would like to add I would like to thank Dr. Kerzan. The Prosecution has no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That -- you took us by surprise. I want to make sure that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the Defence are not caught on the wrong foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Only slightly in that I -- in terms of I have to re-assemble the lectern. I think it came from Ikea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've never seen any lecterns at Ikea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want some time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm fine, I can start straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I would like to add that we have a lectern there ourselves that is completed. If my colleague can handle --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. I can handle it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. As we near the end, I recognise more cooperation between Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kerzan, I'll have a few questions for you and will also involve looking at some of the documents again. To start off with, though, I have some questions arising from your CV and your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it right you currently work for the ministry of the interior?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I work for the -- actually, it's the police. I work for the police lab now for 14 years, as I stated, almost 14 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So your laboratory is a police laboratory and then you work with policemen and prosecutors as your daily work?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes -- well, not only prosecutors. Also we are also sometimes called in as -- for defence. But rarely, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm coming to that. One matter firstly. Are you actually a head of your laboratory or not? I wasn't clear about that.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I'm head of the department of handwriting and document and currency analysis. I'm not the lab -- I'm not the head of the lab.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in the capacity of working in a police laboratory, are you actually able to accept instructions from the defence and to use the facilities of the police in order to analyse material for the defence?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, usually, usually it is the court that asks us to -- now it depends how the other things work. We do work for the police. We do prepare some kind of - how to put that? - pre-reports to the police so the police can act against the accused and so on. We do that no -- I mean, we do that -- I mean, we quite often disappoint the police because they're not happy if we find their conclusions wrong. And then the other -- the other possibilities that the court, either by the motion of the prosecution or the defence ask either the lab to do the expert opinion or they can also -- also turn to me as an expert opinion appointed by the court. So it -- usually, I don't really know who it is, but it -- sometimes I know it is -- whether it is -- we sometimes know whether defence demanded a new opinion or not. Our opinion as a police officers usually are not in the fights of the trial procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So are you able to tell us actually whether you personally have been engaged by the defence, do you actually know whether you have been, or is it only been by the police?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, we were often, either me personally or the lab, appointed by the court. And it is -- we can see from the -- from the court order which party wanted us to prepare or wanted me to prepare a new or a first or a second expert opinion. But it is the court, in the same way as here I was appointed by the court, not either by defence or Prosecution. If I made that clear, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's more or less clear. Thank you. And I think you've told us you've done about 70 analyses as a court-appointed expert. How many of those were analyses of signatures as opposed to handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, there I would say -- it's difficult. Most of them were signatures because when I was appointed by the court usually it involved either -- either a - how do you call that? - inheritance papers, you know when --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Either the will or some contracts where the signatures are involved. Most of them are those.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And how many analyses have you done of signatures in Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: A couple. Not a lot, to be honest, but I do a couple in the last 14 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I omitted one question about your PhD. What's the subject of your PhD?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: The subject of my PhD has nothing to do with the work I do. I did a sociology PhD, as you might have seen in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Now you've also done signature analyses for the Prosecution of this Tribunal in the past. You can confirm that? You're aware that it was for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it was for the Prosecution, as I believe, although as far as I was told back then in the first case, which is the case of Dragan Jevtic, I was not told what it is. I really was not told. I don't know really the procedures here, so it's hard for me to tell which part of the procedure that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we'd like to pass up copies of the report in the Brdjanin case as an exhibit, and for the record the ERN 02295496 to 02295501. Unfortunately we don't have an English version of the report, it's just a one-page summary in English, and -- but, of course, rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record since I was the Presiding Judge in the Brdjanin case and I speak out of memory more than anything else, but I -- although there were a lot of submissions during the course of the trial on the authenticity of certain signatures or documents, the Trial Chamber never came, actually, to hearing evidence on authenticity of signatures. So whatever examinations of signatures may have taken place, that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It never reached the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I want to assure you -- assure you of that. And that's for the record more than anything else. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And it's simply this, really, again, for the record, this is dated 17th of January, 2002, and it is headed ministry of the interior so I take it that you were affiliated with the --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, it's Ministry of the Interior general police department and -- and used to be the -- whether the department of criminal investigation, and then the forensic lab -- the whole -- the whole head of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. It's simply this, actually. I just want to draw your attention to the second page.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's the second paragraph where it says "examination was aggravated because of insufficient comparative material, time gap between disputed and comparative signatures, and the fact that some of the disputed material were photocopies." Now, do you recall writing that?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: You said paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, the first full paragraph in the centre.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Are you referring to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In the English.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, sorry, I was referring to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Oh, my apologies, it's the second page. I'll -- do you recall writing that and do you recall that that was actually -- your examination was aggravated by a seven- to eight-year time gap?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, in this particular case it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I'll ask for an exhibit number for this, please, Your Honour, since I referred to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and this will become Defence Exhibit D --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1022, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1022. Yes, thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We may come back to that later. I want to turn to your report now, if I may, to C7.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Which report?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, your report in this case. You can put that to one side; we'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, okay. C7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's your report. C7 is your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your report, do you have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the original language, Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'm going to be working from the English.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to start just with the statement of your mandate, and I appreciate that as -- the mandate, as you set it out there, was from the wording of this Trial Chamber's order, but nonetheless I want to review it with you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Just tell me on which -- what page to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, well in the English it's page 2 where it says: "The analysis was to determine the following." And the first one is: "Whether the signatures of the questioned documents when compared with the provided reference signatures documents are of the same author." Now, I take it you understood that included in that question is, of course, whether they're not, whether they're not of the same author.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course I understand. It's self-evident I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I want to be clear about that because I think it arises again with the way you express in your conclusions, but is it clear that your mandate was not to assume that the questioned and referenced signatures were by the same author and then to see if the evidence supported that assumption --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I don't really grasp your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Let me approach it a different way and I'll come to the way you stated your analysis results scale, and that's on page 5 in the English. The wording is: "Conclusions strongly support the assumption that the questioned and referenced signatures were written by the same individual."

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My question goes to that really, that you seem to be starting from an assumption, believing that you've been given an assumption that the questioned and referenced signatures are the same, and then you're looking to see if that assumption can be supported, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, first of all it should be a proposition, not assumption. I -- if you check my summary, you would see there, "findings strongly support the proposition," not assumption. That's why it would be good for the translators to use that. "Proposition" is different than "assumption."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading from the English.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I have two propositions, either somebody did write or did not write and I work with these two propositions here, if that clears the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I'm working from the English where it says "assumption," maybe that's a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I have "amended proposition" on all of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Staying with this mandate a bit longer. The second part of the mandate concerned whether there was any tampering, but then again the third part of the mandate whether the questioned documents contain any other feature relevant to establishing their authenticity, and, again, do you understand that would include establishing also their inauthenticity or establishing something that's fishy or wrong about the document and not simply proving authenticity.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, of course I understand that. That's -- basically this question goes in that direction as you pointed it, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask: Did you know when you analysed these documents what the P stood for, P73?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I don't know what P stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you understand that these were Prosecution exhibits?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. You told me that just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to look back at your methodology before moving on to the documents. You explained your methodology today, and it appeared at one point that you were saying that the methodology is the same for analysing handwriting as for analysing signatures. Is -- are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's not entirely the same. I didn't say it was the same. It is the same basis, but signature examination has certain additional problems comparing to handwriting analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the pose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which were explained while -- when I explain it with the fact that the signature is more individualised, can be more simplified, it's the most intimate writing act of the person, that's the reason why you work differently. And I -- as I wrote also somewhere in the report, you can have completely illegible signature but still it's possible to assign it to a person. So that would be a difference between handwriting and signature analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. Jones. I heard at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would appreciate a break between a question and an answer, since the two speakers speak the same language. It's very difficult to interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And I'm sure that both Mr. Jones and Dr. Kerzan will comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So the methodology isn't exactly the same for handwriting and for signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Can I explain the difference that can arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: While in handwriting you almost always have letters to analyse, in signature you just sometimes have lines. It is very nicely stated in a -- in a B/C/S translation with the same word as I used "parafa" [phoen] we use this word. This is completely illegible, but it can be very, very individualised and it can be -- it is -- one is able to -- to identify or -- or prepare opinion with a strongly -- either strongly or not so strongly support some proposition that somebody did or did not write the signature. That is the difference I'm talking about, the reason being, as I stated before, because it is a highly individualised writing act, the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And beyond that, it's also an act which is done more often than other words and it's also something which needs to be consistent because, after all, signatures on a cheque or signatures on a credit card need to be consistent or you risk not having your cheques paid. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, correct, and to be honest I had a lot of troubles with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, consistency is supposed to be, but you have people whose hand -- whose signatures are extremely inconsistent and then you cannot perform a proper examination, unless you have an extremely enormous amount of comparative material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And we're going to come back to that in relation to P269, but for the moment we're just dealing with the introductory part of your report. On page 3 you set out principles of signature examination.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, of course there are more principles than these four, aren't there? This is a simplification?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would say it's -- but these are the main points.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, isn't another very partner principle that you have to have a sufficient sample, otherwise you can't do the job at all?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but I find that's self-evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in fact is the -- is there a fuller list maintained by this European Network of Forensic Handwriting Experts of principles?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I don't think so. It's -- basically I used the -- as you saw -- I think I used most of them or all of them, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I shortened them a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, I want to ask you about at least one of these principles of the examination procedure, and it's at page 5 of your report and it's the penultimate sentence of the first paragraph. And it says -- or you say: "Therefore, special attention must be paid to legibility, size and proportion, slant, pressure, and flow of the signature, et cetera." Now, did you analyse pressure in this case?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, pressure is seen on the paper. You can see the pressure, you can see the pressure of the writing utensil, but the question is which writing utensil you use. If you use fountain-pen, which is most often the case here, the pressure is hardly seen because fountain-pen, as I explained, has liquid ink. Liquid ink goes out of the fountain-pen by itself, [indiscernible], while ball-point pen is something you have to press to start writing. So the difference is big. You don't -- I have quoted here a [indiscernible], what has to be -- special attention has to be paid for. It does not mean always to all of it because sometimes some are not visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, dealing with the reference samples, in fact you couldn't really analyse pressure, could you, because you only had photocopies. So you could analyse -- correct me if I'm wrong. That's what I heard you say earlier, the reference samples.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: The reference samples was photocopied -- photocopies that were signed. The signature itself was original written with a ball-point pen. The signatures were not photocopies. Photocopies was the content of these papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I apologise. That was a misunderstanding. In terms of the reference samples being from a ball-point pen, you said there's actually a difference, isn't there, between pressure used with a ball-point pen and the pressure used with a fountain-pen. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. I have to wait for the transcript. And if you could confirm that again, please -- yes, we have the confirmation. So when it comes to pressure, there's a different pressure as was used in the reference samples from what was used in the -- those questioned signatures which were written with fountain-pen, correct? You're not comparing like with like?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Not exactly, as you pointed. The fact -- fact that you can't see -- you can't see the pressure with a fountain-pen does not mean that it doesn't exist, but you can't see that. That's a slight difference in that. But of course with the fountain-pen, seeing the pressure is far more difficult and is very often nonvisible. Sometimes it is visible when the pressure is lighter, and I showed that when I was asked by the -- by the Judge on a couple of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to ask you about another couple of features that you looked at. Are you familiar with the term "garlanded," "garlanded script"?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that word. It could have been used with the portion which is underlined 6, that would be garlanded writing. I do not use this word, as it has quite different meaning in the history of arts. That's why I don't think it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it what you refer to as wave-like part, when you mentioned wave-like parts which you're analysing. That's garlanded and arcade composition, would that be correct, analysing the loops?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Not entirely. Garland, yes, but arcade, no; arcade is something else. It's quite the opposite. One is going down the other is going up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what I'm wondering. Did you analyse that in these signatures, the wavy parts down and the wavy parts going up?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, before we move on to your sample, I want to ask you about one further analytical question, it's on page 7 of your report, again in the English, that's the third paragraph. And it's just to draw your attention to this point. You analysed reference signatures with what appears to be mathematical precision, the length, 14 to 18 millimetres, the average angle of slant. Forensic document examination is not an exact science, is it?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, it is not. I was trying to see the ratios between certain parts; that is all. It is not mathematical, no, it is far from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, have you heard of David Ellen?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to read just a section from his book, and we have copies for everyone. It's at page 46. Let me just get it in front of me before we move on. The book is "The Scientific Examination of Documents, Methods, and Techniques." It's the second edition. It's page 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We haven't copied the whole book; we've copied the extracts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now -- yes, page 46, there's a section which says "subjectivity." You can probably see the heading there.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'll just read that paragraph. It says, "In any assessment of evidence derived from examination of documents which depends not on mathematical conclusion but on the evaluation of the significance of all the findings taken in combination, there must be a subjective element as well as a possible variation in observation of the documents in question and an awareness of the background knowledge of the subject, there may be elements within the personality of the expert which play a part, a tendency to caution or the opposite perhaps. In addition, there will be variations in the competence of the examiners." Now, do you agree with that, that forensic document examination is not a science based on mathematical conclusion, but there is an element of subjectivity?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with you and that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the personality of the examiner has a tendency of caution or the opposite, plays a role as well?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It's hard not to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To the extent that you do use mathematical parameters, the point is, is it not, that if a questioned signature falls outside those parameters that that's a difference worth noting -- that that's a difference, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, you have to realise that -- that it is not the exact measurements that you measure. I did the measurements here; I agree with you. It's obvious. But the point is a person can have a lot of place for his signature; he can have a small place. But usually the proportions should stay within the same limits, more or less. They can go out a bit but not a lot. That's -- that's why I did the measurement, to -- I didn't want to fool anybody with that, to -- that this is some kind of a very precise thing. I think I wrote that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then the question is: How much -- when something falls outside the parameters, whether that's enough to be significant or not, and that's a matter for your judgement?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the same applies, does it not, to what is natural variation, or what is attributable to natural variation, and what might be a forger doing a bad job?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to samples now, and I think again we might have a quote from David Ellen. Do you agree that it's of fundamental importance to have a comparative sample that's sufficient in both quantity and quality in order to do analysis?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: That comes without saying, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to just read from page 63 of Ellen, and it's in chapter 5, handwriting, the collection of samples. And it's -- yes, sorry. Yes, paragraph 3. "There are two essential requirements before any material is adduced as a standard for specimen of known writing. One is that the writing must be adequate in quantity and quality for the examination to be carried out." And then it continues. I'm just concerned with that and you've agreed with that proposition. Now, if we turn to page 67 at the very bottom where we see signatures and it says there: "Signatures are important as known writings written in the course of business. A wide variety of these, written without the knowledge that they may be later used as comparative material, gives a better indication of the whole range of variation used by the writer than a small sample taken at one sitting." Now, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, your comparative sample, the reference signatures, was a small sample, was it not, eight signatures, taken at one sitting, on one date, the 23rd of May, 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down please for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, that's one factor that the reference signatures are taken in one day. Now, is it also the case that you had eight questioned signatures and there were more -- my apologies. Eight referenced signatures, but you had more questioned signatures, 11, and is it -- you'll obviously agree with that, but isn't there a principle that you shouldn't be looking at more questioned signatures than you have referenced signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, I have never heard of that principle -- am I too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you don't agree?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, it depends when we go to the -- to the reference signatures, it's the absolute number of the -- those which is important. Of course it is good to have more of them as less than them. But there are differences how many of those are needed. It goes down to five to six to, I remember writing -- to I remember somebody wrote at least ten times as much as the questioned -- the questioned sample. Of course if you have a couple of hundreds of questions, it's hard to have ten times more. It is not that important. It is -- but more you have, better it is. But eight are somewhere in the middle of -- they should be enough in most of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, in fact isn't eight close enough to being not enough at all in that you said it goes down to -- five to six, I take it, is the minimum you would require, referenced signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's not a lot of those. It's close to the -- to the limit. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on top of that, we have the fact that these are from nine years later from the actual questioned signatures, and did that not in Brdjanin, in the Brdjanin report we saw, that was actually something which posed a problem to analysis. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: One of the problems, if I may say. I don't really remember this case very good -- it's really four years ago. I don't remember the signatures, but the main problem was that I had only three -- three reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: And so that was the main problem in this case. But also the time lapse can be a problem, and I have it written down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to come back to that because I think that merits more detail. Isn't it also the case that these signatures, reference signatures, were given in artificial circumstances and in an artificial place, at the top of the document in a confined space?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, the fact that they are on the top of the document I don't really find very important. But I fully agree that those specimens were taken with -- I believe with the -- with the -- as to be used for examination, I believe. I may be wrong, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: But it is far better to have signatures that were taken for any other reason, so to -- so to speak. And I can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just for the record. I do believe that my learned friend didn't invite the expert to speculate on this, but this was rather a speculation. And I would like -- rather than to request the Court to be alert on the matter, as this is a pure speculation from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are alert, Mr. Wubben, and I also think that the witness, too, is alert. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I can clarify with one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think you need to. We understand the question and we also understand what his answer was. So let's move. I mean, he was not there present when these signatures were taken in any case. So he cannot be in the mind of whoever asked for those signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I just wanted to ask one further question on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These weren't signatures which were at the bottom of a, say, contract or a birth certificate or some document that you come across in the normal state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I'll have to read that. I don't really understand what you are asking for. Those signatures were at the top of the page. They are not at the typical place; I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me clarify. We saw a moment ago in David Ellen where he talks about signatures are important as known writings written in the course of business. And I don't want you to speculate, and if you can't answer this, then don't. But as far as you can tell were these signatures written in the normal course of business?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Which signatures?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: The reference signatures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. We've dealt with the fact that those reference signatures were in a ball-point pen, and you were comparing that with fountain-pen pen in some instances; that, too, hinders analysis, does it not?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: It can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And considering all of that, wouldn't you agree that you had a very poor sample in terms of quantity and quality?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Are you talking about a sample of reference materials?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. It's not a poor sample. I would be more than happy to have more of that, but I'm always more than happy if I have more. But the samples itself are relatively, relatively good. They're written with the fluency, they're written -- executed nicely. As I said before, it is a very nice -- I mean, nice, I like that signature. It's a nice signature, nicely balanced, and those signatures, those referenced signatures were such. So I don't think when -- when assessing the signature you just don't go by the -- whether there are numbers -- numbers are enough, whether they are taken in this sort of way. You have to look at the signatures to assess whether they are -- whether they are good for -- for examination. It's not just the -- whether there is five, four, or ten of them or a couple hundred of them, if you understand what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I do, but surely when you have more signatures you might notice something which you didn't notice before, that perhaps a certain mark is much more predominant in that person's signature than appeared in the reference sample simply because it was unrepresentative. That's surely a risk if you have a small quantity?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: That's always a risk even if you have a large quality, but with a small quantity this risk can be larger, bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And finally on this issue, I did say want to come back to the issue of the nine-year gap.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Could you speak slower?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I have been asked by the stenographer to do that as well, so obviously I have to make an effort. If you turn to page 7 of your report, now there you comment on this -- this nine-year gap and you say "there is a difference of nearly nine years between the time that the questioned and referenced samples were created. Although this is quite significant for the purposes of signature analysis, it is not sufficient to render the examination impossible." Now, my question is: That's not the point, is it? It's not that it makes it impossible; the point is, it makes it more difficult, doesn't it, a nine-year gap. Ideally you would like to have signatures two years, three years, four years afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, there are no rules how old the signatures should be. As new -- as close to the questioned signatures the referents are, the better it is, of course. What is meant here -- what I meant here is, of course there is this time gap of nine years, but within nine years the signature can change but it does not change with -- with all the people. I remember cases when I had -- when I had one particular case when I had handwriting from the -- I think just after World War II. It was an engineer who wrote exactly the same way 40 years later. It can happen that way or somebody can change his signature within a year or handwriting. It can happen. It depends on the age of the person. It depends on the different -- for example, legal status, and so on. I was talking about the marriage at this point. So there's a lot of -- it's just an obstacle that has to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you had reference signatures from 1996, 1999, 2001, 2003, a spread, do you accept that you might have reached different conclusions if you had signatures, reference signatures, from a broader period of time?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: I cannot deny the possibility of that; of course I cannot deny, but I'm quite confident that my opinion was in this way prepared as it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly. I don't question that. Maybe I should put it this way. If you had signatures from 1996, let's say, three or four signatures from then, some from 1998, wouldn't your examination have been more complete and more accurate?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case I would say it would be better if they were from 1992. I would prefer them from 1992. Of course that can change the -- the examination, but it is not something that is a rule in this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to move to your analysis results scale on pages 5 to 6 of your report and ask you a few questions about that scale. Now, you told us -- you told us today that the -- this European network uses this scale and uses the terms strongly supports the proposition, et cetera, that it's the same author. But it doesn't recommend the additional step you take of then giving an opinion that it is the same author of the reference and question signatures. Is that correct? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me correctly. I refer now to the summary, if I may. In the summary, page 2, you will have -- you will have the -- I'll just have -- I will just explain it on the first -- for the first step on the scale of conclusions. "Findings strongly support" and so on and so on to the end of -- not comma -- what's that. From the point "therefore in my opinion," that's mine. The rest of it is a quote from the ENFHEX collaborative exercise scale of conclusions, which we -- which I use daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, that network is an eminent network, I take it? It's a respected body of experts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: As to my knowledge, there's no other body to be -- to be so distinguished in Europe as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I suggest to you that the reason why they don't recommend this wording of going on to say that in one's opinion the referenced signatures and the questioned signatures are the same when they've reached the conclusion that it strongly supports the conclusion, is because that's illogical, it's an illogical step to go from strong suggestion to what appears to be a definite conclusion. I'll put it again if you don't follow.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Just, did you say illogical or logical step, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Illogical.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Illogical step.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me approach it this way, let me put it again to you. You've done your analysis. You conclude that there are enough features to strongly support the proposition that the questioned and referenced signatures are written by the same individual, but rather than stopping there you then go to the next step and give an opinion which appears to be definite. It appears to be a clear conclusion that it's the same person. I suggest to you that is not logical.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, yes. I have to explain that in terms of what we do in your legal system. In our legal system, the -- now I'll have problems with wording, to be honest. But we have -- every opinion comprises of two parts. One is part which is, let it put in quotes, objectively done. So this is the description and all of the -- what you see, what you -- your annotations, and so on. I think you understand what I mean. I hope you understand. And then there's opinion. Opinion at the end is a subjective -- subjective -- subjective assumption or -- do not please catch me by the word because it's very difficult to explain that. This is my subjective -- this is subjectively, I say -- under these circumstances -- after this examination I think so. I did not say "I know that." It's a bit of a difference here, but this is not illogical. If findings strongly support a conclusion, the conclusion can be on the other hand -- can be concluded. But this is the opinion of subjective nature. The last -- at the last sentence is this, where we were talking about subjectivity. This is my subjective opinion. If I answered you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, we need to dwell on that a little?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Strongly supports is not the same thing as a definitive, hundred per cent conclusion then, is it?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: No, and I never said that -- if I say it's my opinion that it has something to do with hundred per cent. If you think the opinion is hundred per cent -- I don't know, I don't find opinions hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So do you leave the possibility and when you reach of a conclusion of that nature that in fact the document is not written by the same author as those of the reference samples. That's a possibility even when you give that opinion?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Well, in any opinion this possibility cannot be ruled out. I just believe that in particular cases -- in any particular case I can assess whether this is a large or small possibility. In this particular case I believe that this possibility is very, very small. That is what is meant by opinion; it is not meant that that is a fact of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I also want to develop this a bit more with a suggestion which I'll be putting to you, that of course the signatures which we've been looking at, and we'll come to specifics subsequently, but of the questioned and reference samples, of course they look similar. My suggestion to you is that they look the same because it's the work of a seasoned professional forger who's practiced the signature of the -- of Naser Oric so that he can do it almost perfectly, so that it can become a habitual movement of the forger. Now, can you exclude, categorically exclude, the possibility that for those documents where you've given the opinion that it's the same author, that in fact it's the work of a seasoned, professional forger? Can you exclude that?

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: As I said before, there's no hundred per cent opinions, and I cannot exclude anything like that. But I believe that the consistency, the fluency of these signatures shows quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DORIJAN KERZAN
utterances.text: Those that were told that way. There are some that are quite inconclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to come to the documents one at a time. I just was speaking, of course, generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, more or less where do you stand because my idea was to finish in a few minutes' time, more or less. If it's -- I don't know how long you require to clear this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to proceed document by document after -- after two or three questions on another issue, but I'm perfectly happy to break now and resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I think it would be also wiser to do that, give you the opportunity to consult with your expert, and we can resume. Do you think you will finish tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. My estimate is an hour, an hour and a half tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Then can I ask you to be -- continue to be cooperative, as you have already been so far today, and try and sit down and exchange information on the documents that we need to discuss after we finish with the testimony of the witness which require something else to be done like certain documents that we still haven't got the CD from your part, and certain documents that -- anyway. I mean, if you exchange the information, it will make the exercise much simpler when we come to it. MR. DI FAZIO: Do you mean housekeeping matters not related to this topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, not related to the same, no, housekeeping, I mean, because, as I said, that's why I asked Mr. Jones whether he -- it's likely that he finishes his cross-examination tomorrow because I anticipated that to be the case. And if we can finish tomorrow as well, then it will be much, much better. And we can do this housekeeping exchange for as long as needed. We could go the following day if necessary. And if there is an exchange of information in the meantime, it will be much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will exercise the contact with Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just one question, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kerzan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent tomorrow the questions will be, but would it be wise for me to see the opinions of the Prosecution and Defence to prepare myself for tomorrow or I shouldn't?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would it be possible to know it after I finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Curiosity killed the cat, Dr. Kerzan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I just mention one matter in that regard. I think I put on the exhibit list a page from our report. It was purely for visual comparison, but I thought better of that idea today and I'll use his images instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact you anticipated an intervention that I had in my mind, actually, as to whether it was regular to use that or -- anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I won't use that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to mention it at this stage, particularly considering what you've just stated. So, Dr. Kerzan, go and have a good rest. Tomorrow you've got a couple of hours still with us, and then you're free to go home unless the Prosecution embarks on a re-examination which will last a week. I also -- you can -- Madam Usher, you can escort Dr. Kerzan. Tomorrow also will be the last time we will see Mr. Wubben in this courtroom in his role as lead counsel for the Prosecution. And when we finalise the exercise, the testimony plus the exercise, I had in mind to have a very short ceremony here and it's the concluding part of the public sitting tomorrow. I just wanted to alert you to this fact so as not to be surprised. I thank you so much. Have a nice evening and we'll -- tomorrow, by the way, we have shifted the sitting for the morning, okay? To the morning. You're both aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.
